title: Vomiting Blood After Drinking: Causes and When to Go to the ER
excerpt: Threw up blood after drinking? What bright red streaks, clots, and coffee-ground vomit usually mean, the common causes, and when to go to the ER right away.
metaDescription: Vomiting blood after drinking? What red streaks and coffee-ground vomit mean, common causes like Mallory-Weiss tears, and when to go to the ER.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
> **Get emergency care now (read this first).** This article is general information, not medical advice. **Call 911 or go to the emergency room right away if** you vomit more than a small amount of blood, you see clots, the vomit is dark brown or black like coffee grounds, you have black, sticky, or tarry stools, or you feel dizzy, lightheaded, faint, very weak, confused, short of breath, cold and clammy, or have a racing heart, chest pain, or severe belly pain. **Also go to the emergency room if** you have liver disease or have been told you have cirrhosis or varices, you take blood thinners, or the vomiting won't stop. **Get seen the same day** (urgent care, your doctor, or the ER) if you noticed only a few thin streaks of blood and feel otherwise well. If someone has passed out and is vomiting, roll them onto their side and call 911.

**The honest answer first:** vomiting blood after drinking always deserves a medical check, and in most cases that means going to an emergency room now rather than waiting to see if it stops. Very often the cause is a small tear in the lining where your food pipe meets your stomach, torn by hard, repeated retching, and many of those heal on their own. But you can't tell at home whether you're looking at a small tear or a serious bleed, and serious bleeds can get worse quickly. This page explains what the different kinds of blood in vomit usually mean, the common causes after a night of drinking, what happens at the hospital, and what to do (and not do) while you get help.

**The quick rules:** If you see more than a streak of blood, the vomit looks like coffee grounds, your stools are black, or you feel dizzy, faint, weak, short of breath, or have chest or belly pain, **call 911 (or your local emergency number) or go to the nearest emergency room now.** Don't drive yourself. If it was only a thin streak and you feel otherwise fine, still get seen the same day. Stop drinking, don't take ibuprofen or aspirin, and don't wait until tomorrow to see if it happens again.

## What Vomiting Blood After Drinking Usually Means

Doctors call vomiting blood **hematemesis**. It means bleeding is happening somewhere in the upper part of your digestive tract: your mouth or throat, your food pipe (the esophagus), your stomach, or the first part of your small intestine (the duodenum).

Alcohol plays into this in two main ways. First, it irritates the lining of the stomach and esophagus directly, which can leave it raw, inflamed, and more likely to bleed. Second, heavy drinking often ends in forceful, repeated vomiting and dry heaving, and that pressure can physically tear the lining. A third, much more serious route applies mainly to people who have drunk heavily for many years and have liver damage: swollen veins in the esophagus that can burst.

For a social drinker who overdid it on one night, the most likely explanations are the first two. That's reassuring in one sense, because those are often treatable and many heal on their own. But "most likely" is not the same as "safe to ignore." Bleeding from the upper digestive tract is one of those situations where the appearance doesn't reliably tell you how bad it is, so the standard advice from health services like the NHS and major hospital systems is the same: get it checked.

## Is It an Emergency? How to Read What You're Seeing

The color and amount of blood give doctors useful clues. They are not a substitute for being examined, but they help you understand how urgent things are.

| What you see | What it often means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| Bright red blood, more than a streak, or clots | Active bleeding that is happening now | Call 911 or go to the ER now |
| Dark brown or black flecks that look like coffee grounds | Blood that has sat in the stomach and been darkened by acid; bleeding may have been going on for a while | Go to the ER now, or same-day care at the very least if you feel completely well |
| Black, sticky, tar-like stools | Digested blood passing through the gut, a sign of upper digestive bleeding | Go to the ER now |
| A few thin red or pink streaks after hard retching, and you feel fine | Often a small tear or irritated lining, but can't be confirmed at home | Stop drinking and get seen the same day |
| Pink or red vomit that matches what you drank (red wine, punch) | Possibly dye or drink, not blood | If you're not sure, treat it as blood and get checked |

How you feel matters as much as what you see. Dizziness when you stand up, fainting, a fast heartbeat, pale or clammy skin, and unusual tiredness can mean you've lost enough blood to affect your circulation. Those are emergency signs even if the amount of blood you saw looked small, because some bleeding stays inside the gut and never comes up.

## The Common Causes of Vomiting Blood After Drinking

### Mallory-Weiss tear (a tear from retching)

A **Mallory-Weiss tear** is a tear in the inner lining where the esophagus joins the stomach. It is classically linked to bouts of forceful vomiting or retching, and binge drinking is one of the textbook triggers. The typical story is a person who throws up several times, keeps dry heaving, and then notices fresh red blood in later vomits.

The good news is that most Mallory-Weiss tears stop bleeding on their own and heal within a few days. The reason you still need to be seen is that some bleed heavily, and doctors may need to stop the bleeding during an endoscopy (a camera passed down the throat). They will also want to rule out the other causes on this list, because the story can look the same at first.

### Alcohol-related gastritis

**Gastritis** means inflammation of the stomach lining. Alcohol is one of its well-known causes, especially in larger amounts. When the lining is inflamed it can develop small raw patches, called erosions, that ooze blood. That blood might show up as streaks, as coffee-ground material, or occasionally as black stools.

Gastritis from a single heavy night often settles once you stop drinking and let the stomach rest, sometimes with acid-reducing medicine from a doctor. If you've been having burning stomach pain after drinking for a while, our guide to [stomach pain after drinking](/never-hungover/stomach-pain-after-drinking) explains what's going on and what helps.

### Esophagitis and acid damage

Alcohol relaxes the valve at the top of the stomach and can increase acid, which lets acid wash up into the esophagus. Repeated vomiting adds more acid exposure. The result can be **esophagitis**, an inflamed, raw food pipe that may bleed a little. People often notice heartburn, pain when swallowing, or a sore chest along with it. If heartburn is a regular part of your nights out, see our guide to [heartburn after drinking](/never-hungover/heartburn-after-drinking).

### Stomach or duodenal ulcer

An **ulcer** is an open sore in the lining of the stomach or the first part of the small intestine. The two big causes are infection with a bacterium called *H. pylori* and regular use of NSAID painkillers such as ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin. Alcohol is not usually the root cause, but it can irritate an existing ulcer and make bleeding more likely.

This is where the hangover routine can quietly make things worse. Taking ibuprofen or aspirin for a pounding head, on an irritated stomach, after a night of drinking, stacks three stomach irritants together. US labels for these medicines warn about stomach bleeding for people who have 3 or more drinks a day for that reason. Our pages on [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol) and [aspirin and alcohol](/never-hungover/aspirin-and-alcohol) go into the details.

An ulcer that bleeds can lose a lot of blood, sometimes with little pain beforehand. Black stools, coffee-ground vomit, or feeling faint are the warning signs.

### Esophageal varices (mainly in people with liver disease)

Long-term heavy drinking can scar the liver (cirrhosis). That scarring raises pressure in the veins that carry blood through the liver, and blood backs up into veins in the esophagus and stomach. Those veins swell into **varices**, which have thin walls and can burst. A bleeding varix can cause large amounts of bright red blood and is a life-threatening emergency.

Most social drinkers don't have this problem, but some people have liver disease without knowing it. If you've been told you have cirrhosis, fatty liver that has progressed, or varices, or you notice yellow skin or eyes, a swollen belly, or easy bruising, any blood in your vomit is a 911 situation.

### Esophageal rupture (rare but serious)

Very rarely, violent vomiting can tear all the way through the wall of the esophagus. This is called **Boerhaave syndrome**. It usually causes sudden, severe chest or upper belly pain after vomiting, sometimes with pain in the neck or shoulder, trouble breathing, and feeling very unwell. Blood in the vomit may be small or absent. It is a surgical emergency, so severe chest pain after vomiting means calling 911, whether or not you see blood.

### Blood that didn't start in your stomach

Not every red streak comes from the gut. Swallowed blood from a nosebleed (alcohol widens blood vessels, and dry air and rubbing can set one off), bleeding gums, a cut in the mouth, or a raw throat from repeated vomiting can all turn up in vomit. These are usually minor. But it's hard to be sure where blood came from, so if you didn't clearly have a nosebleed or mouth injury, get checked.

## Things That Look Like Blood but Aren't

After a night out, the stomach can contain a lot of things that are red, pink, or dark. Common lookalikes include:

- **Red wine**, sangria, and red or pink cocktails
- **Fruit punch**, cranberry juice, and red sports drinks
- **Red-dyed foods and candy**, tomato sauce, beets, or red peppers
- **Coffee, cola, or chocolate**, which can look dark brown
- **Yellow or green bile** when your stomach is empty, which is not blood (bile is common after repeated vomiting)

For stools, **bismuth subsalicylate** (the active ingredient in Pepto-Bismol) and **iron supplements** can turn stool black, which can look like the tarry stool of a bleed. It's worth mentioning to a doctor if you've taken either.

The safe rule is simple: if you can't be confident it's food or drink, assume it's blood and get checked. Emergency staff deal with false alarms all the time and would much rather see you than miss a bleed.

## What to Do Right Now

If you or a friend has just vomited blood:

1. **Decide how urgent it is.** Use the box at the top of this page. If there's more than a streak, any coffee-ground material, black stools, or any dizziness, fainting, chest pain, or severe belly pain, call 911 or go to the ER now.
2. **Don't drive yourself.** Bleeding can make you lightheaded, and you may still be over the limit from drinking. Have someone take you, or call an ambulance.
3. **Stop drinking.** No more alcohol tonight, including "hair of the dog" in the morning.
4. **Don't eat or drink much until you're seen.** Small sips of water are fine if you're not vomiting, but doctors may want an empty stomach for an endoscopy.
5. **Skip painkillers.** No ibuprofen, naproxen, or aspirin. Don't take anything for the hangover until you've been checked.
6. **Note what you saw.** The color, roughly how much, how many times, and whether you'd been retching hard first. A photo can help, even if that feels awkward. Also note what you drank, any medicines you take (especially blood thinners, steroids, or painkillers), and any liver problems you know of.
7. **If someone is very drunk and vomiting,** keep them on their side so they don't choke, stay with them, and call 911 if they can't be woken, are breathing slowly or irregularly, have blue or pale skin, or are having a seizure. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, which is an emergency in its own right.

## What Not to Do

- **Don't wait until morning to "see if it happens again."** Bleeding from the upper gut can be slow and hidden, and you may feel worse later.
- **Don't take ibuprofen, naproxen, or aspirin.** They can make stomach bleeding worse.
- **Don't drink more alcohol** to settle your stomach.
- **Don't force yourself to vomit** to "clear it out." More retching can widen a tear.
- **Don't assume it's just the red wine** if you aren't certain.
- **Don't feel embarrassed.** Doctors see alcohol-related vomiting constantly. Being honest about how much you drank helps them treat you properly.

## What Happens at the Emergency Room

Knowing what to expect can make it easier to go. The details depend on the hospital and how you look when you arrive, but the general approach to bleeding in the upper digestive tract is well established.

**First, they check how stable you are.** Staff will look at your pulse, blood pressure, and breathing, and ask about how much blood you saw and how you feel. If you've lost a lot of blood, they'll start fluids through a drip and may give a blood transfusion.

**Then come blood tests.** These usually include a blood count to see if your hemoglobin (the oxygen-carrying part of your blood) has dropped, tests of how well your blood clots, and kidney and liver tests. Your hemoglobin may look normal at first even after a bleed, which is one reason they may repeat it.

**They may give acid-reducing medicine.** A type of drug called a proton pump inhibitor is commonly given, sometimes through a vein, to lower stomach acid and help bleeding stop.

**An endoscopy is often the key test.** A doctor passes a thin, flexible camera through your mouth into your esophagus, stomach, and duodenum to find where the blood is coming from. If there's an active bleed, they can often treat it during the same procedure with clips, an injection, or heat. You're usually given sedation, so it's less unpleasant than it sounds. Depending on how stable you are, it may be done the same day or within the next day or so.

**Some people go home the same day; others stay.** If the bleeding was small, has stopped, and your tests are reassuring, you may be sent home with medicine and follow-up plans. Larger bleeds, liver disease, or unstable vital signs usually mean a hospital stay. Doctors use scoring systems that weigh your blood tests, blood pressure, and symptoms to help make that call.

## Streaks of Blood After Throwing Up: Do Small Amounts Matter?

This is the most common version of the question, and it's understandable to want to wait it out. A few thin streaks after a long bout of retching often come from a small Mallory-Weiss tear or a raw throat, and many of these heal without treatment.

The trouble is that the first vomit with blood doesn't tell you whether the bleeding is about to stop or get worse. That's why the safest plan is still to be seen the same day, even if you feel fine. Urgent care or your own doctor may be enough for a single small streak with no other symptoms, though many will send you on to an ER to be safe. Go straight to the ER if:

- the streaks keep appearing with each vomit
- you see clots, a larger amount, or coffee-ground material
- you have black stools
- you feel dizzy, faint, weak, or your heart is racing
- you have chest pain, especially severe pain after vomiting

## Vomiting Blood the Morning After Drinking

Sometimes the blood doesn't appear until the next day, during a hangover. That can happen when an irritated stomach lining keeps oozing overnight, when a tear from the night before reopens with more retching, or when blood that collected in the stomach overnight comes up later. In that last case it's often darker or looks like coffee grounds, because it has had time to mix with stomach acid.

The advice is the same as at night: treat it as a reason to get checked today. It's also a good moment to look at what else is going on. If you also have black stools, severe stomach pain that spreads to your back, yellow skin or eyes, or you can't keep any fluids down, those point toward problems that need care quickly.

If you're vomiting repeatedly the morning after but there's no blood, our guide to [hangover nausea](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025) covers safe ways to settle your stomach and rehydrate.

## Recovery and Drinking Again

Recovery depends entirely on the cause, which is another reason a diagnosis matters.

- **A small Mallory-Weiss tear** usually heals within days. Doctors may give acid-reducing medicine and suggest a bland diet for a short time.
- **Gastritis or esophagitis** often improves over days to weeks with acid-reducing medicine, food, and a break from alcohol.
- **An ulcer** usually needs a course of acid-reducing medicine, a test for *H. pylori* (and treatment if it's present), and a hard look at how often you use NSAID painkillers.
- **Varices or liver-related bleeding** is a long-term medical issue that needs specialist care, and doctors will usually advise stopping alcohol completely.

On drinking again: wait until the doctor who treated you says it's safe. Alcohol can irritate a healing lining and restart bleeding. If a doctor finds liver disease or an ulcer, their advice about alcohol may be very different from the general advice for healthy social drinkers, so ask directly.

If you notice that nights out often end with heavy vomiting, or you find it hard to stick to your own limits, that's worth raising with your doctor too. They can talk through options without judgment.

## How to Lower the Risk Next Time

Most vomiting blood after a single night of drinking traces back to the same chain of events: too much alcohol, too fast, often on an empty stomach, followed by repeated, forceful vomiting. Breaking that chain is the most effective thing you can do.

- **Pace yourself.** The body clears roughly one standard drink an hour (this varies a lot from person to person). Drinking faster than that is when nausea and vomiting usually start.
- **Eat before and while you drink.** Food slows how fast alcohol reaches your bloodstream and protects your stomach lining to some degree. See our guide to [drinking on an empty stomach](/never-hungover/drinking-on-an-empty-stomach) for why it hits so much harder.
- **Alternate with water.** It slows your drinking pace and helps with the dehydration that vomiting makes worse.
- **Stop when you feel queasy.** Nausea is a clear signal to stop drinking, not to push through.
- **Avoid NSAIDs around drinking.** Don't take ibuprofen, naproxen, or aspirin before bed after a heavy night or first thing in the morning on an empty, irritated stomach.
- **Be careful with very strong or acidic drinks** if you already have heartburn or a sensitive stomach.
- **Know your own history.** If you've had an ulcer, reflux, or liver problems, you have less margin for error, and your doctor may suggest you drink less or not at all.

After any episode of heavy vomiting, focus on gentle rehydration once you're able to keep fluids down. Small sips of an oral rehydration drink or water with a little salt and sugar can help replace what you lost; our page on [electrolytes and alcohol](/never-hungover/electrolytes-and-alcohol) explains how.

## Can a Supplement Help?

No. No supplement, hangover product, or home remedy treats or prevents vomiting blood. If you have vomited blood, the right move is to get medically checked and to stop drinking until a doctor tells you the cause has healed.

## The Bottom Line

Vomiting blood after drinking is never something to sleep off. The most common causes in social drinkers, a small tear from retching and an inflamed stomach lining, are often treatable and many heal quickly. But they look a lot like more serious causes at first, and the amount of blood you see doesn't reliably show how much you're losing. Call 911 or go to the emergency room for anything more than a streak, any coffee-ground vomit, black stools, or any dizziness, fainting, chest pain, or severe belly pain. For a single small streak with no other symptoms, stop drinking and get seen the same day. Skip ibuprofen and aspirin, don't drive yourself, and don't drink again until a doctor says the cause has healed.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is vomiting blood after drinking an emergency?**

Treat it as one until a doctor says otherwise. Health services such as the NHS advise going to an emergency department or calling emergency services if you vomit blood. A few thin streaks after hard retching are often from a small tear that heals on its own, but you can't safely tell that apart from a serious bleed at home. Go straight away if there is more than a little blood, the vomit looks like coffee grounds, your stools are black, or you feel dizzy, faint, short of breath, or have chest or belly pain.

**Why would I throw up blood after a night of drinking?**

The most common reasons are a Mallory-Weiss tear (a small tear in the lining where the food pipe meets the stomach, usually caused by forceful retching) and alcohol-related gastritis (an irritated, inflamed stomach lining that can ooze blood). Less often it comes from a stomach or duodenal ulcer, especially if you also take ibuprofen or aspirin. In people with liver disease from long-term heavy drinking, it can come from swollen veins in the food pipe, which is a life-threatening emergency.

**What does coffee-ground vomit mean?**

Vomit that looks like dark brown or black coffee grounds usually means blood has been sitting in the stomach long enough for stomach acid to darken it. It points to bleeding in the upper digestive tract that may have been going on for a while. It needs urgent medical care the same day, and an emergency visit if it comes with dizziness, fainting, black stools, or a racing heart.

**Is a small streak of blood in vomit after drinking normal?**

It's common, but it isn't something to shrug off. Thin streaks after repeated retching often come from a small tear or irritated lining and many settle within a few days. Still, get checked promptly, ideally the same day. Go to the emergency room if the streaks keep coming, the amount grows, you see clots or coffee-ground material, or you feel weak, dizzy, or faint.

**Could it be red wine or a red drink instead of blood?**

Yes, it can. Red wine, fruit punch, red sports drinks, cranberry juice, red cocktails, and foods like beets or tomato sauce can all make vomit look red or pink. Swallowed blood from a nosebleed or bleeding gums can also show up in vomit. If you are not sure, assume it is blood and get checked. Doctors can test for blood and would much rather see a false alarm than a missed bleed.

**Can I drink alcohol again after vomiting blood?**

Not until a doctor has found the cause and told you it has healed. Alcohol irritates the stomach lining and can restart bleeding. Many small tears and mild gastritis heal within days to a few weeks, but an ulcer or liver-related bleeding changes the advice entirely. Ask the doctor who treated you when, and whether, it's safe to drink again.

**Should I take ibuprofen or aspirin after vomiting blood?**

No. Ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin (NSAIDs) can irritate the stomach lining and make bleeding more likely, and their labels already warn about stomach bleeding for people who have 3 or more drinks a day. Don't take any painkiller until you've been checked. If you need something for a headache later, ask the doctor or pharmacist which option is safe for you.
